pr_title: Remove Uri scheme validation from HttpRequestMessage
pr_body:
Fixes #52836

Removed the Uri scheme check from `HttpRequestMessage` / `HttpClient.BaseAddress` and moved it in `SocketsHttpHandler.ValidateAndNormalizeRequest`.

Any scheme will be passed to handlers.

~~No merge: Should other handlers have filters for specific schemes?
`WinHttpHandler` takes 85 seconds to figure out it can't process `foo://httpbin.org` without a fail-fast like this for example.~~
Added `http` / `https` checks to `WinHttpHandler`.

> No merge: Should other handlers have filters for specific schemes?
WinHttpHandler takes 85 seconds to figure out it can't process foo://httpbin.org without a fail-fast like this for example.

Yeah, we should add the same logic to WinHttpHandler.

With this PR:
- HttpRequestMessage does not throw on any Uri
- SocketsHttpHandler behavior remains the same (http, https, ws, wss)
- WinHttpHandler only accepts http and https
- BrowserHttpHandler will receive any Url (any absolute scheme + any relative)

@lewing is this the desired behavior for Browser, or should we be filtering out relative Uris?

> How does JavaScript or something else communicate with such endpoints?
> 
> That will answer the question if it is something `HttpClient` in WebAssembly might want to support or not.

The extensions://* is chrome or the chromium system's private "extends manager protocol"
it's full string is :  chrome-extension://\<extensionID\>/\<pathToFile\>
extensionID is target extendsid, 
path to file is the relative path about the extends folder.

You can think that is chromium's private file protocol, like file:\\.....
It seems inappropriate for generic framework like .NET HttpClient to worry about other product private guts. It seems like some kind of external package would be much more appropriate.

CC @marek-safar @kjpou1 @lewing we should consider if it makes sense to explicitly support things like this for browser.

The check is also in `HttpRequestMessage` which will reject any Uri scheme except for:
`http`, `https`, `ws`, `wss` and (for browser) `blob`.
If this boils down to schema check only, I think we could loosen the restriction for wasm.

@scalablecory Yeah, just as @MihaZupan  mentioned, for now, it block me in HttpClient.BaseUri and HttpRequestMessage.Uri, and even WebRequest.Create.
So there is no way for me to send that request to the schema in C# class. I must skip the checking by reflection as I metioned above.

> If this boils down to schema check only, I think we could loosen the restriction for wasm.

Yeah, I'm not sure what the point of checking this in HttpClient/HttpRequestMessage themselves is. 

The underlying HttpClientHandler will enforce whatever schemes it knows how to handle. Limiting this at the HttpClient/HttpRequestMessage layer seems unnecessary.

Let's keep the check only in Handler.

review_comments: Do we have similar validation for all of the above in place for WinHttpHandler and the BrowserHttpHandler used on wasm?
Not in managed code from what I can tell
It seems like these are still things that should be checked regardless of handler.
Though I suppose it's probably also good to check them here, in case we are being used without HttpClient...

We ensure that the Uri is not null and IsAbsolute in [HttpClient](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/ca00588105feae898bc73b6d24bf9600d41b39db/src/libraries/System.Net.Http/src/System/Net/Http/HttpClient.cs#L744), but we didn't do that in the handler directly.
I will add the check to WinHttpHandler as well.

Do we care to have the IsAbsolute check in Browser as well? I don't know if passing a relative Uri to it works / does anything useful.

> Do we care to have the IsAbsolute check in Browser as well?

@lewing?

The browser does support relative URIs. It could even support `null` URIs if they were treated like an empty string but they currently aren't. Relative URIs are resolved against `location.href` automatically by the browser:
https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/97898a4c9292d91a8e4f4b6add67f66f66f661b3/src/libraries/System.Net.Http/src/System/Net/Http/BrowserHttpHandler/BrowserHttpHandler.cs#L244-L246

To clarify, when using `HttpClient`, relative Uris will not be allowed through.

Where a user can get to calling `BrowsersHttpHandler` with a relative Uri is if they create the handler themselves and use an invoker instead of client:
```c#
using var invoker = new HttpMessageInvoker(new HttpClientHandler());
await invoker.SendAsync("relative Uri");
```

So if that does something meaningful, we should just let the browser decide what to do?


Side note:
`BrowsersHttpHandler` should most likely be calling
```c#
requestUri.IsAbsolute ? requestUri.AbsoluteUri : requestUri.ToString()
```
instead of just `ToString()` on the Uri.
Why do we disable telemetry if the Uri isn't absolute?

The call to `RequestStart` that follows this check will access Uri fields that would throw for relative Uris.

Adding this check here so that you get the meaningful exception message from `SocketsHttpHandler` instead.
